## Introduction

A transition network summarises many sequences in one matrix of
transition probabilities (Saqr et al., 2025; Saqr, López-Pernas, & Tikka,
2025a; Tikka, López-Pernas, & Saqr, 2025). Whether a centrality ranking, a path or a group difference read
from that matrix holds beyond the sample depends on how much the matrix
changes when the data change, and on whether the model's assumptions hold
(Saqr, López-Pernas, & Misiejuk, 2026a; Misiejuk et al., 2026). Nestimate
(Saqr, López-Pernas, & Misiejuk, 2026b) assesses a network in eight ways,
and cograph draws the networks.

| Question | Function |
|----------|----------|
| How precisely is each edge estimated when sequences are resampled? | `bootstrap_network()` |
| How precisely do the observed counts determine each edge? | `certainty()` |
| Which edges remain when the uncertain ones are removed? | `net_prune()` |
| Do two random halves of the data give the same network? | `network_reliability()` |
| Do the edge weights hold when sequences are dropped? | `casedrop_reliability()` |
| Does the centrality ranking hold when sequences are dropped? | `centrality_stability()` |
| Does the next state depend only on the current one? | `markov_order_test()` |
| Which edges are large as probabilities but small as counts? | `magnitude_difference()` |

## Data

`ai_long` holds the coded AI turns of 428 human-AI pair-programming
("vibe coding") sessions, one row per action: 8,551 actions, each coded as
one of eight AI actions. Vibe coding, programming by conversation with an
AI assistant (Sarkar & Drosos, 2025), has been studied with transition
networks, which describe what the student and the AI do in turn (Saqr,
Misiejuk, & López-Pernas, 2026). The network holds one sequence per session, ordered by
`order_in_session`.

```{r data}
library(Nestimate)
library(cograph)
net <- build_network(ai_long, method = "relative", action = "code",
                     actor = "session_id", time = "order_in_session")
state_frequencies(net)
```

`Execute` (38%), `Investigate` (27%) and `Plan` (19%) make up most of the
actions; `Ask` (1.2%), `Report` (2.1%) and `Repair` (3.0%) are rare. An edge
leaving a rare action is estimated from few transitions.

```{r network}
net
extract_initial_probs(net)
```

The strongest transitions are from `Delegate` to `Plan` (0.62) and from
`Execute` to itself (0.51). Most sessions open with `Investigate` (72%).

```{r network-plot, fig.height = 6}
splot(net)
```

## Bootstrap

`bootstrap_network()` resamples the sessions with replacement, re-estimates
the network in each resample, and reports for each edge its mean, its 95%
percentile interval and a p-value (Efron, 1979; Saqr et al., 2025). With
the default `inference = "stability"`, the p-value is the share of
resamples in which the edge falls outside 0.75 to 1.25 times its estimate,
so a significant edge keeps its size; with `inference = "threshold"` it is
the share in which the edge falls below `edge_threshold`, so a significant
edge is present.

```{r bootstrap}
boot <- bootstrap_network(net, iter = 1000, seed = 1)
boot
head(summary(boot), 8)
```

21 of the 64 edges keep their size in 95% of the resamples. The
strongest edges are estimated precisely: `Execute` to `Execute` has a 95%
interval of [0.48, 0.53]. Edges from rare actions are wider: `Ask` to
`Explain`, estimated from the 99 transitions out of `Ask`, has an interval of
[0.38, 0.60] and is significant only at the 5% level.

`splot()` draws the significant edges solid and the others dashed; the
forest plot shows every edge's estimate and interval, ordered by size,
with the significant edges marked.

```{r bootstrap-plot, fig.height = 6}
splot(boot)
```

```{r bootstrap-forest, fig.height = 12}
plot_bootstrap_forest(boot, show_ci = TRUE)
```

The width of an interval follows how often its source action occurs: the
median width is 0.08 for the edges leaving `Ask` and `Report`, the two
rarest actions, against 0.015 for `Execute` and 0.014 for `Investigate`,
the two most frequent.

```{r bootstrap-threshold}
bootstrap_network(net, iter = 1000, seed = 1, inference = "threshold",
                  edge_threshold = 0.05)
```

26 edges stay above 0.05 in 95% of the resamples. The two rules answer
different questions: whether an edge exists, and whether its size is
estimated precisely.

## Bayesian certainty

`certainty()` gives each edge a posterior distribution instead of
resampling. The transitions out of each action are modelled as a
Dirichlet-multinomial process: with a Dirichlet prior added to the counts,
each edge probability has a Beta posterior, so its mean, standard
deviation and credible interval are computed exactly (Johnston &
Jendoubi, 2026). The default prior, 0.5 added to every cell, is the
Jeffreys prior (Jeffreys, 1946). An edge is certain under the same two
rules as in the bootstrap, with the posterior mass in place of the share
of resamples.

```{r certainty}
edge_certainty <- certainty(net)
edge_certainty
head(summary(edge_certainty), 8)
```

26 edges are certain against 21 significant in the bootstrap; the two
agree on 57 of the 64 edges. The credible intervals are narrower than the
bootstrap intervals (median width 0.043 against 0.048), because the
posterior treats every transition as independent, while the bootstrap
resamples whole sessions and so includes the differences between them.
The more the sessions differ from each other, the wider the bootstrap
intervals are relative to the credible intervals.

`certainty()` returns the same layout as `bootstrap_network()`, so the
same plots draw it.

```{r certainty-plot, fig.height = 6}
splot(edge_certainty)
```

```{r certainty-forest, fig.height = 12}
plot_bootstrap_forest(edge_certainty, show_ci = TRUE)
```

## Pruning

`net_prune()` removes edges from the network. `method = "bootstrap"`
removes the edges the bootstrap finds non-significant; `"disparity"`
keeps the edges that carry a larger share of their state's outgoing
weight than expected when the weight is spread at random over the state's
edges (Serrano, Boguñá, & Vespignani, 2009); `"threshold"` removes the
edges below a fixed weight. Self-loops are never removed.

```{r prune}
pruned <- net_prune(net, method = "bootstrap", boot = boot)
summary(pruned)
summary(net_prune(net, method = "disparity", level = 0.05))
```

The bootstrap keeps 27 of the 64 edges: the 19 significant edges between
different actions and the 8 self-loops. The disparity filter at the 5%
level keeps 16, the edges that take a large share of their row.

```{r prune-plot, fig.height = 6}
splot(pruned)
```

## Split-half reliability

`network_reliability()` splits the sessions at random into two halves,
estimates the network in each, and compares the two weight matrices: the
mean, median and largest absolute difference between corresponding edges,
and the correlation of the edge weights.

```{r reliability}
reliability <- network_reliability(net, iter = 500, seed = 1)
reliability
plot(reliability)
```

Over 500 splits, the edge weights of the two halves correlate at 0.97 on
average (SD 0.01), and corresponding edges differ by 0.023 on average. The
largest difference in a split averages 0.14. The histograms show the
distribution of each measure over the splits.

## Edge stability under case-dropping

`casedrop_reliability()` drops increasing proportions of the sessions,
re-estimates the network, and correlates its edge weights with those of
the full data. The CS-coefficient is the largest proportion that can be
dropped while the correlation stays above 0.7 in 95% of the resamples
(Epskamp, Borsboom, & Fried, 2018).

```{r casedrop}
edge_stability <- casedrop_reliability(net, iter = 200, seed = 1)
edge_stability
plot(edge_stability)
```

The CS-coefficient is 0.90, the largest proportion tested: with 90% of the
sessions removed, the edge weights still correlate at 0.85 on average with
those of the full data. `summary()` returns the same measures per drop
proportion with their quantiles.

```{r casedrop-summary}
head(summary(edge_stability), 9)
```

## Centrality stability under case-dropping

`centrality_stability()` drops sessions in the same way and correlates
the centralities of the reduced data with those of the full data, one
CS-coefficient per measure. Epskamp et al. (2018) suggest that the
CS-coefficient should not be below 0.25 and preferably above 0.5.

```{r centrality}
centrality <- centrality_stability(net, measures = c("InStrength",
                                                     "OutStrength",
                                                     "Betweenness"),
                                   iter = 200, seed = 1)
centrality
plot(centrality)
```

In-strength and out-strength reach 0.90 and betweenness 0.70: the
rankings by strength hold with 90% of the sessions removed, the ranking by
betweenness with 70%. Betweenness depends on which shortest paths exist
and changes more when a few edges change.

## Markov order

A transition network is a first-order Markov model: it assumes the next
action depends only on the current one. `markov_order_test()` tests at
each order *k* whether order *k* describes the sequences better than order
*k* − 1. The statistic is a likelihood ratio $G^2$; its null distribution
comes from permuting the next action within each context of the preceding
*k* − 1 actions. The permutation is conditional rather than exact, because
the overlapping windows of one sequence are not independent (Besag &
Mondal, 2013).

```{r markov-order}
markov_order <- markov_order_test(net, max_order = 3, n_perm = 200, seed = 1)
markov_order
plot(markov_order)
```

The AIC and the BIC both select order 1. The permutation test rejects
every order up to 3: each observed $G^2$ lies above all 200 permuted
values (p = 0.005, the smallest possible with 200 permutations), so it
selects order 3. At order 3 the asymptotic chi-square p-value is 0.35,
because most of the 1,470 degrees of freedom belong to contexts that occur
a few times; the permutation null does not rely on that approximation.
The previous action carries most of the information, and longer histories
add some that the criteria judge not worth their parameters.

## Counts and probabilities

The network gives each edge as a probability, the share of a state's
transitions that go to another state. A frequency network gives it as a
count (Saqr, López-Pernas, & Tikka, 2025b). An edge leaving a rare state
can be a large probability and a small count. `magnitude_difference()`
estimates both networks, rescales the counts to the range of the
probabilities, and returns the difference per edge.

```{r magnitude}
magnitude <- magnitude_difference(ai_long, action = "code",
                                  actor = "session_id",
                                  time = "order_in_session")
magnitude
summary(magnitude, n = 8)
```

The median difference is 0.03, and 9 of the 64 edges differ by more than
0.2. The largest differences all leave rare actions: `Delegate` to `Plan`
is a probability of 0.62 but 0.07 on the count scale, `Ask` to `Explain`
0.48 against 0.02, and `Repair` to `Execute` 0.47 against 0.05.

```{r magnitude-plot}
plot(magnitude)
```

Each sector is one source action. The grey part of a wedge is the value
both views share, and the coloured tip the difference.

## Summary

| Assessment | Result for `ai_long` |
|------------|----------------------|
| Bootstrap, edges keeping their size | 21 of 64 |
| Bayesian certainty, certain edges | 26 of 64; agrees with the bootstrap on 57 |
| Edges kept by bootstrap pruning | 27 (19 between actions, 8 self-loops) |
| Split-half correlation of the edge weights | 0.97 |
| Edge CS-coefficient | 0.90 |
| Centrality CS-coefficients | in-strength 0.90, out-strength 0.90, betweenness 0.70 |
| Markov order | AIC and BIC: 1; permutation test: 3 |
| Edges differing by more than 0.2 between counts and probabilities | 9 of 64, all from rare actions |
